title: Electric cars and buses
titleCn: 电动汽车与电动巴士的发展

paragraphs.text: Part four. You will hear a design technology student called Donna Williams presenting the findings of her investigation into the development of vehicles run on electricity.
First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

Good morning, everyone. For my project, I decided to look not at a brand new technology, but at what I regard as an ingenious application of an existing technology, which was in the development of buses and cars which run on electricity.

Now, lots of you will probably be surprised that I chose this topic because I'm not familiar with the field at all. But when I was looking around for a subject, I accidentally came across a feature article reviewing the work of engineer Howard Ross. I was struck by how accessible the science behind these new vehicles was, and it gave me confidence to investigate further.

Some of you will also be saying, "Well, haven't electric cars and buses been around for ages? What's so innovative about them?" Well, yes, but as you know, they haven't really caught on. As I see it, the main reason for this, and I'm speaking very much as a non-scientist, mind you, is that in the past, vehicles were stuffed with huge batteries to stop them grinding to a halt every few miles. Ross's solution is to recharge vehicles as they actually drive along, so their batteries need only be of modest dimensions. A plate fitted to the bottom of the vehicle sucks energy from the electrical power points located beneath the surface of the road, which are called charging strips.

The basic technology for this system has been around for years. For example, some electric toothbrushes and hand drills use it, but nobody has seen that it could, without too much effort, be used for ecologically friendly transport.
But getting down to what I'm really interested in, development and applications. How likely is it that people will give up their dependence on the internal combustion engine and choose electricity?
Well, a diesel engine apparently wears out after about five thousand hours, but electric vehicles should still be going strong after twenty thousand hours.
Not that I think it'll be that which will convince people to make the switch. I think it'll be because the annual fuel bill could be reduced by sixty percent.
Sadly, the obvious fact that this technology is much cleaner and healthier for us all will probably be of only secondary importance.
How likely is it that this technology will even make it to the market?

Well, they are still in the development stage, but from what I've read, if anyone's going to make it happen, it'll be Howard Ross. I was so impressed by his passion for the project. It's this that has already persuaded several businesses to sponsor further trials.

The article reported on one trial for the bus, which I found particularly interesting. Initially, they'd done several runs with the bus over different types of terrain, um, flat, bumpy, up and down hill, et cetera, but they hadn't had any passengers in it. When people came into the picture, boarding the bus and altering the distance between the bus and road, they had to revise their planning.

So let's have a closer look at the two vehicles Ross has developed, the bus and the car. They both use the same basic technology, but with interesting modifications to suit their different needs. Starting with the bus. The charging strips are only five meters long, but are placed at bus stops, so the vehicle is charged while the passengers are boarding and paying and so on, and so the charging doesn't significantly hold up progress. Now, these electric buses have been extensively trialed already, principally at a university, because it provided a limited circuit that could be followed. And the only remaining operational concern is that the magnetic field might damage credit cards being carried by passengers.

Obviously, that's something that'll have to be ironed out [laughs]. And the cars. Obviously, your average car owner won't want to be stopping every two miles to recharge. So Ross has developed much longer charging strips of approximately three hundred meters, which are placed at an average of every three kilometers.

Now, the cars haven't been trialed as much as the buses, for obvious reasons. It's much more difficult to lay such long charging strips. But Ross has managed to lay the strips on parts of the road near his home. They have been extremely successful, although one trial did indicate that there may be problems with interference with TV stations in the immediate area.
One more problem to address in the later-
That is the end of part four.
You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
